title: testward: How Often Do Old Tests Fail on Merged Agent Pull Requests, and Does It Matter?
description:
A pre-registered kill test for a merge gate. testward replays a pull request's pre-existing tests, at their base-branch version, against the merged code, and asks for a human sign-off when one that passed on the base now fails. The study asked whether that event is common enough, and rarely enough intended, to justify the gate.

Data. 447 merged agent-authored pull requests from the AIDev dataset (Python repositories, two random samples with fixed seeds); each was replayed by running the base-branch tests against both the base and the merged code, and 170 gave a conclusive replay.

1. The event is common. Old tests fail on the merged code in 62 of 170 conclusive replays (36.5 percent, 95 percent CI 29.6 to 43.9).

2. It is rarely a problem. Two raters labelled all 62 independently (agreement 54 of 62); every disagreement and every unclear case was traced read-only through the repository's history. Result: 59 intended behaviour changes and 3 real undisclosed regressions (4.8 percent, CI 1.7 to 13.3). Two are stale agent branches merged over newer work; one dropped a read-only tool check. No case was found of an agent weakening a test to hide its own failure.

3. The gate is killed by its own pre-registered rule: 95.2 percent of flags are intended changes, against a bar of under 50 percent. The replay remains useful as information for a reviewer, not as a gate.

Limits: half the replays were inconclusive (mostly dependencies that did not install), merged pull requests only, Python and pytest only, no human comparison group. The repository holds the pre-registration, deviations, every replay row, both raters' labels and the agreement report.
